---
title: "Simulation study: do the weights recover known effects?"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, out.width = "100%")
res <- read.csv("simulation-results.csv", check.names = FALSE)
se <- read.csv("simulation-se.csv", check.names = FALSE)
show <- function(prefix) {
  tab <- res[startsWith(res$scenario, prefix),
             c("method", "truth", "mean", "bias", "mcse", "emp.sd", "rmse", "reps")]
  knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Method", "Truth", "Mean estimate", "Bias", "MCSE of bias",
                             "Empirical SD", "RMSE", "Replications"))
}
show_se <- function(prefix) {
  tab <- se[startsWith(se$scenario, prefix),
            c("method", "mean.est", "mean.se", "emp.sd", "se.ratio", "coverage", "mcse.cov", "reps")]
  knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Method", "Mean estimate", "Mean SE", "Empirical SD",
                             "SE / empirical SD", "Coverage of 95% CI", "MCSE of coverage",
                             "Replications"))
}
```

This article checks, by simulation, whether the new features of ipw do what
they should: each scenario generates data in which the true causal effect
is known, estimates it, and repeats this hundreds of times, in the spirit of
the simulated example in the JSS paper (van der Wal & Geskus 2011).

**Main findings**

* **The new weights remove confounding when their model is correct.** Naive
  analyses and weights from misspecified models are biased by 15% to over
  200%; the new weights reduce this to 0 to 5%.
* **The remaining small biases (3 to 5%) are properties of inverse
  probability weighting, not of the implementation.** Weights computed from
  the true model (*oracle* weights) have the same bias for log-normal doses,
  and for smooth terms and ordinal exposures the bias shrinks as the sample
  grows.
* **`ipwboot()` gives accurate standard errors when the weights are well
  behaved**, where robust standard errors are 8 to 10% too large. It does
  **not** fix analyses with extreme weights: with poor overlap or long
  products of time-varying weights, no standard error reaches 95% coverage,
  and the bootstrap is then not better than the robust standard error.

**How the results were produced.** The study is in
[`dev/simulation-study.R`](https://github.com/TranHung93/ipw/blob/main/dev/simulation-study.R);
the code below shows the essential lines of each scenario. It takes about 20
minutes on 4 cores, so this page shows saved results. To reproduce them, run
`Rscript dev/simulation-study.R` in the package folder (seed 20261101,
L'Ecuyer random numbers, 4 parallel workers), or start the `simulations`
workflow from the GitHub Actions tab. Replications: 500 for scenarios 1 to 4,
250 for 5 and 6, 200 for the large-sample and oracle checks, 1000 for 7a and
7b, and 500 for 7c and 7d, each with 200 bootstrap samples.

**Reading the tables.** *Bias* is the mean estimate minus the truth. The
*MCSE* (Monte Carlo standard error) shows how precisely the simulation
estimates that bias: a bias within about 2 MCSE of 0 could be simulation
noise. *Empirical SD* is the spread of the estimates; *RMSE* combines bias
and spread.

```{r bias-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 9}
d <- res[!grepl("median", res$method), ]
d <- d[rev(seq_len(nrow(d))), ]
lab <- paste0(sub("\\..*", "", d$scenario), ". ", d$method)
type <- ifelse(grepl("oracle", d$method), "oracle",
         ifelse(grepl("misspecified|unweighted|adjustment|truncated", d$method), "other", "new"))
rel <- d$bias / abs(ifelse(d$truth == 0, 1, d$truth))
cap <- 1
op <- par(mar = c(4, 24, 1, 1))
plot(pmax(pmin(rel, cap), -cap), seq_along(lab), yaxt = "n", ylab = "",
     pch = c(new = 19, oracle = 17, other = 1)[type],
     xlab = "Relative bias (bias / |truth|)", xlim = c(-cap - 0.2, cap + 0.2))
axis(2, at = seq_along(lab), labels = lab, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.62)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)
out <- abs(rel) > cap
if (any(out)) text(ifelse(rel[out] > 0, cap, -cap), which(out), sprintf("%.2f", rel[out]),
                   pos = ifelse(rel[out] > 0, 4, 2), cex = 0.65)
legend("bottomright", pch = c(19, 17, 1), bty = "n", cex = 0.75,
       legend = c("new weights", "oracle weights (true model)", "naive, misspecified or truncated"))
par(op)
```

# 1. ATE, ATT and overlap weights, and `ipwprob()`

The effect of a binary exposure varies with the confounder `l`, so the three
estimands differ. Their true values, from 2 million simulated people, are
ATE = 1.00, ATT = 1.27 and ATO = 0.86. Each weighting scheme is compared with
its own target; `ipwprob()` is given the true propensity scores.

```{r eval = FALSE}
d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$a <- rbinom(1000, 1, plogis(0.5 + 0.8 * d$l))
d$y <- d$a * (1 + d$l) + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.att <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  denominator = ~ l, data = d, estimand = "ATT")$ipw.weights
coef(lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = w.att))["a"]
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("1.")
```

All weighted estimates are within 1% of their own estimand; the unweighted
difference is twice the ATE.

# 2. Count exposures: Poisson or negative binomial

Each extra unit of a count exposure raises the outcome by 0.5. In 2a the
counts are overdispersed (negative binomial); in 2b they are Poisson.

```{r eval = FALSE}
d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$v <- rnbinom(1000, size = 2, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$l))   # 2b: rpois(1000, exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$l))
d$y <- 0.5 * d$v + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.nb <- ipwpoint(exposure = v, family = "negbin", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("2")
```

With the correct model, both families are within 1.5% of the truth. The
Poisson model applied to overdispersed counts over-corrects as strongly as
the unweighted analysis under-corrects. The negative binomial model remains
usable for Poisson data (bias 3.6%), so it is the safer choice when in doubt.

# 3. Skewed continuous exposures: gaussian, gamma or log-normal

One unit of dose raises the outcome by 1. In 3a the dose is log-normal given
`l`, in 3b gamma. In 3a the true densities are known, so *oracle* weights
(the true marginal density over the true conditional density) show what
weighting can achieve without any estimation error; they are also computed
for a 5 times larger sample.

```{r eval = FALSE}
d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(2000))
d$dose <- exp(0.5 + 0.5 * d$l + rnorm(2000, 0, 0.6))   # 3b: rgamma(2000, 3, 3 / exp(0.5 + 0.3 * d$l))
d$y <- d$dose + 2 * d$l + rnorm(2000)
w.ln <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "lognormal", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
oracle <- dlnorm(d$dose, 0.5, sqrt(0.61)) / dlnorm(d$dose, 0.5 + 0.5 * d$l, 0.6)
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("3a")
show("3b")
```

The correct family removes most of the confounding (unweighted bias 54% and
76%). The 3 to 5% that remains is **the same for oracle weights** (5.0% vs
4.9% at n = 2000, 3.4% vs 3.2% at n = 10000), so it does not come from
estimating the model: it is the finite-sample bias of weighting with
densities of a skewed exposure, whose density ratios have a heavy tail, and
it shrinks slowly as the sample grows. The gaussian model is clearly worse,
and in 7 of 500 replications gave infinite weights, which `ipwpoint()`
refuses. A misspecified skewed family (gamma for log-normal data or the
reverse) has a small bias but up to twice the spread. Truncation reduces the
spread a lot but adds bias.

# 4. Curved propensity: smooth terms with mgcv

The probability of exposure depends on `l` through a sine curve; the true
effect is 2. Oracle weights use the true propensity.

```{r eval = FALSE}
d <- data.frame(l = runif(2000, -2, 2))
d$a <- rbinom(2000, 1, plogis(2 * sin(1.5 * d$l)))
d$y <- 2 * d$a + 3 * sin(1.5 * d$l) + rnorm(2000)
w.gam <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ s(l), data = d)$ipw.weights
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("4.")
```

A straight-line logistic model leaves a quarter of the confounding bias.
With `s(l)` the bias is 3.6% at n = 2000 and 1.5% at n = 10000: it halves as
the sample grows five-fold, as expected for a smoothing estimate that
approaches the true curve. Oracle weights are unbiased, which confirms that
the remaining bias comes from estimating the curve.

# 5. Time-varying exposure, `type = "all"`

## 5a. Ordinal dose

A dose level (0, 1, 2) is chosen at each of 4 visits from a proportional-odds
model given the confounder `L` and the previous dose. `L` is affected by the
previous dose and by an unmeasured `U` that also affects the outcome; the
outcome rises by 1 per unit of cumulative dose. This is the situation in the
JSS paper where ordinary adjustment fails.

```{r eval = FALSE}
for (t in 1:4) {
  l <- U + 0.4 * prev + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
  dose <- findInterval(0.8 * l + 0.6 * prev + rlogis(n), c(0, 1.5))   # 0, 1, 2
  prev <- dose
}
y <- cumulative.dose + 2 * U + rnorm(n)
w <- ipwtm(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
           numerator = ~ dose.lag, denominator = ~ dose.lag + l,
           id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
# weight at the last visit, then lm(y ~ cumulative.dose, weights = ...)
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("5a")
```

Both naive analyses are biased (+49% and -14%). Ordinal and multinomial
weights recover the effect; the 2.5% bias of the ordinal weights at 500
people falls to 1.4% at 2500, and oracle weights are within 1%.

## 5b. Smooth terms in `ipwtm()`

A binary exposure is chosen at each visit with a curved effect of `L`
(logit = -0.3 + 2 sin(1.5 L) + 0.6 × previous exposure), in the same design.

```{r eval = FALSE}
w <- ipwtm(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit", numerator = ~ a.lag,
           denominator = ~ a.lag + s(l), id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("5b")
```

Here a straight-line model is worse than no weighting at all: its weights
turn the effect of +1 into a negative estimate. With `s(l)` the bias is 5.5%.

# 6. Recurrent exposure events, `family = "survival"`, `type = "all"`

## 6a and 6b. Weights against the true weights

Exposure events (for example new prescriptions) happen repeatedly with a
known proportional hazard: baseline 2 per unit time, log hazard ratio 0.5 for
a fixed covariate `x` and -1 for a time-varying covariate `xt`. Because the
true hazard is known, the true weights are known too. In 6a all people share
a grid of 10 intervals (as in `haartdat`); in 6b the events happen in
continuous time, `xt` changes at different times for each person, and each
event ends an interval (start-stop data cut at events, as in Graffeo et al.
2018).

```{r eval = FALSE}
w <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", denominator = ~ x + xt,
           id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "all", data = d)
coef(w$den.mod)
median(abs(log(w$ipw.weights / true.weights)))
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("6a")
show("6b")
```

The Cox coefficients are unbiased in both designs, and the estimated
weights are typically within 7 to 9% of the true weights, which is the
estimation noise of the baseline hazard.

## 6c. Causal effect of the number of exposure events

Exposure events happen in continuous time with hazard 1.5 exp(0.6 L). `L` is
updated at 4 visits, is lowered by earlier events (as treatment raising CD4
lowers the need for more) and depends on an unmeasured `U` that also affects
the outcome. The outcome rises by 1 per event.

```{r eval = FALSE}
w <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l,
           id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "all", data = d)
# weight at each person's last row, then lm(y ~ number.of.events, weights = ...)
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("6c")
```

The weights reduce the bias from 80% (unweighted) and 22% (adjustment for
`L`) to 3.4%. The method of Graffeo et al. uses, for an interval ending in an
event, the probability of an event during that interval; this simulation
shows that the approximation works for estimating a causal effect.

# 7. Standard errors: `ipwboot()`, robust and naive

Each table shows the mean estimated standard error divided by the actual
spread of the estimates (1 is ideal) and the coverage of 95% confidence
intervals.

## 7a and 7b. Linear MSM for a binary exposure

True effect 10, n = 500, stabilized weights. In 7a, exposure probabilities
are mostly between 0.1 and 0.9 (good overlap); 7b is the simulated example
of the JSS paper, where many people are almost certain to be exposed or
unexposed.

```{r eval = FALSE}
msm.effect <- function(dd) {
  w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit", numerator = ~ 1,
                denominator = ~ l, data = dd)$ipw.weights
  coef(lm(y ~ a, data = dd, weights = w))["a"]
}
ipwboot(d, msm.effect, R = 200)
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show_se("7a")
show_se("7b")
```

With good overlap the bootstrap standard error is accurate (ratio 1.01, Wald
coverage 94.7%), while the robust standard error is 10% too large (coverage
96.7%), in line with Austin (2016); percentile intervals cover slightly less
than 95%. In the JSS example the estimate itself is biased (11.0 instead of
10) and all standard errors are 38% too small, so coverage is below 60%
whatever method is used.

## 7c. Weighted Cox MSM

Austin (2016) studied weighted Cox models. Here event times are exponential
with hazard 0.1 exp(-0.7 a + 0.8 l), censored at 5; n = 1000. The true
marginal log hazard ratio, -0.624, is computed from both potential outcomes
of 200,000 people (it differs from -0.7 because hazard ratios are not
collapsible).

```{r echo = FALSE}
show_se("7c")
```

All three standard errors are close to the truth here. The robust standard
error is again too large (+8%); the naive one (+4%) and the bootstrap (-3%)
are within simulation noise of 1. With stabilized weights and good overlap,
the bootstrap therefore brings no clear gain over the naive standard error
in this setting.

## 7d. Time-varying exposure, bootstrap by person

The design of scenario 5 with a binary exposure; `ipwboot(id = id)` resamples
people with all their visits.

```{r eval = FALSE}
ipwboot(long, tv.effect, id = id, R = 200)
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show_se("7d")
```

Neither method is adequate here: the bootstrap standard error is 34% too
small and the robust one 26% too small, with coverage of 79% and 84%. The
weights are products over 4 visits, so a few people get very large weights
and the estimate has a heavy-tailed distribution that 500 people do not
represent well, the same problem as in 7b. Truncation, a larger sample or a
better-balanced design would be needed; the bootstrap does not repair it.

# Conclusions

The simulations support the new models: with the correct model, each of
them removes nearly all confounding, and the small biases that remain are
either shared by weights from the true model or shrink with the sample size.
They support `ipwboot()` for analyses with well-behaved weights, where it
gives accurate standard errors and robust standard errors are conservative.
They also show its limit: when weights are extreme (poor overlap, long
products of time-varying weights), no standard error is reliable, and the
first step is to examine the weights (`summary()`, `ipwplot()`) and consider
overlap weights, truncation or a different model.

# References

* Austin PC (2016). Variance estimation when using inverse probability of
  treatment weighting (IPTW) with survival analysis. *Statistics in
  Medicine* 35, 5642-5655.
* Graffeo N, Latouche A, Geskus RB, Chevret S (2018). Modeling time-varying
  exposure using inverse probability of treatment weights. *Biometrical
  Journal* 60, 323-332.
* Li F, Morgan KL, Zaslavsky AM (2018). Balancing covariates via propensity
  score weighting. *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 113,
  390-400.
* van der Wal WM, Geskus RB (2011). ipw: An R package for inverse probability
  weighting. *Journal of Statistical Software* 43(13), 1-23.
